::: {.callout-note title="Goals for this chapter"}
- Describe the structure of the blood-gas barrier and the pulmonary capillary bed, and say how each suits gas exchange.
- Apply Fick's law to predict how area, thickness, gradient, solubility and molecular weight change gas transfer.
- Explain why CO~2~ diffuses about 20 times faster than O~2~.
- Explain why the diffusing capacity (D~L~) depends on the capillary blood (hemoglobin and capillary volume) as well as on the barrier.
- Distinguish perfusion-limited from diffusion-limited transfer, using N~2~O, CO and O~2~.
- Explain how a thick barrier, exercise and altitude make O~2~ transfer diffusion limited.

Names, dates and the exact values in figure captions are context, not things to memorize.
:::

The [Alveolar Ventilation](ventilation.qmd) chapter brought O~2~ from ambient air to the alveolus, where PAO~2~ is about 100 mm Hg. This chapter takes it across the blood-gas barrier into the pulmonary capillary blood, a distance of well under a micrometer that still takes a whole lecture. The next chapter ([Transport of O~2~ and CO~2~](o2-co2-transport.qmd)) covers what hemoglobin does with the O~2~ once it arrives.

Diffusion is passive. No pump or transporter in the barrier moves O~2~ or CO~2~, and no energy is spent. Each gas moves only down its own partial pressure gradient. Keep one question from the last lecture in mind as you read: if alveolar and arterial PO~2~ are both about 100 mm Hg, where is the gradient that drives O~2~ into the blood?

## A barrier built for exchange

**It is thin.** On an electron micrograph of a pulmonary capillary, the barrier has two sides. On the *thin side*, the alveolar epithelium and the capillary endothelium share one fused basement membrane, and the whole barrier is only 0.2 to 0.3 µm thick. Most gas exchange happens there. On the *thick side* there is more interstitium, with bundles of collagen between the epithelium and the endothelium. Edema fluid collects first on the thick side, which spares the thin side for a while (you met edema formation in [Microcirculation](../cardiovascular/microcirculation.qmd)).

**It is large.** The lung has several hundred million alveoli. Repeated branching into acini packs a surface of about 50 to 100 m^2^ into the chest, roughly half a singles tennis court.

**The capillaries are a sheet, not tubes.** In the systemic circulation, capillaries are usually drawn as separate tubes between an arteriole and a venule. In the alveolar wall the capillaries are so densely interconnected that blood flows as a sheet about one red cell thick, a little like a waffle fry, with flow in every direction through the side channels. The aggregate cross-sectional area is large, so resistance is low and blood moves slowly. At rest a red cell spends about 0.75 s in a pulmonary capillary, and at any moment only about 70 mL of blood is in the whole capillary bed, spread across that huge surface.

Small holes in the alveolar walls, the *pores of Kohn*, connect neighboring alveoli. They allow collateral ventilation, so an alveolus whose airway is blocked can still get some air from its neighbors. They are also one path by which bacteria and fluid spread from alveolus to alveolus in lobar pneumonia.

## Fick's law of diffusion

The rate at which a gas crosses a sheet of tissue (V̇~gas~) is proportional to the area of the sheet (A), to a diffusion constant for that gas in that tissue (D), and to the partial pressure difference across it (P~1~ − P~2~), and inversely proportional to the thickness (T):

$$\dot{V}_{gas} = \frac{A \cdot D}{T}\,(P_1 - P_2)$$

This has the same shape as Ohm's law: flow equals a driving pressure divided by a resistance, with T/(A·D) playing the part of the resistance. The lung maximizes A and minimizes T. @fig-diffusion-barrier shows the thickness term at work: with the same gradient, a barrier half as thick has a profile twice as steep and moves twice as much O~2~.

![Barrier thickness in Fick's law. Both barriers have the same gradient, PO~2~ 100 in alveolar gas and 40 in capillary blood. Halving the thickness doubles the slope of the PO~2~ profile across the barrier and doubles the transfer. Fibrosis and interstitial edema thicken the barrier. Course figure.](figures/diffusion/barrier-thickness.svg){#fig-diffusion-barrier}

### The diffusing capacity, D~L~

In a patient you cannot measure the area or the thickness of the barrier. So for clinical work the area, thickness and diffusion constant are lumped into one number, the *diffusing capacity of the lung* (D~L~):

$$\dot{V}_{gas} = D_L\,(P_1 - P_2)$$

D~L~ is a property of the lung and of the gas in question. It does not depend on the partial pressures. You calculate it from a measured transfer and a measured gradient, but if you double the gradient the transfer doubles and D~L~ stays the same.

Now the question from the start of the chapter. If P~1~ is alveolar PO~2~ and P~2~ is arterial PO~2~, and both are 100, the equation seems to say no O~2~ moves. The gradient is *along the capillary*. Blood enters at a PO~2~ of about 40, so at the start of the capillary the gradient is about 60 mm Hg. It shrinks as the blood loads O~2~ and is close to zero a third of the way along. P~2~ is the capillary PO~2~, averaged along the capillary, not the arterial value.

::: {.callout-note title="If you are comparing with the slides"}
Slide 8 writes Fick's law for the lung as V̇~gas~ = D~L~ (P~A~ − P~a~), with arterial PO~2~ as P~2~. In a normal lung P~A~ and P~a~ are about equal, so read P~2~ as capillary partial pressure averaged along the capillary, as the slide 8 notes explain. The course map writes D~L~ (P~1~ − P~2~). Both give the same D~L~.
:::

## What sets D: solubility and molecular weight

The diffusion constant depends on the gas:

$$D \propto \frac{\text{solubility}}{\sqrt{\text{molecular weight}}}$$

A gas that dissolves well in the barrier crosses it faster, and a lighter molecule diffuses faster. The solubility that counts here is solubility in the barrier, which is mostly water. Physical solubility in water or plasma ranks the gases the same way, and @fig-diffusion-solubility shows those values.

**Why CO~2~ diffuses about 20 times faster than O~2~.** CO~2~ is about 24 times as soluble as O~2~. It is also heavier (molecular weight 44 against 32), which slows it a little: √(44/32) ≈ 1.17. So CO~2~ diffuses about 24 ÷ 1.17 ≈ 20 times faster. Molecular weight alone would favor O~2~; solubility outweighs it. In practice this means CO~2~ is almost never diffusion limited, and a high PaCO~2~ is not explained by a diffusion problem. A high PaCO~2~ means hypoventilation.

![Physical solubility of three gases: dissolved gas against partial pressure, measured in blood. The slope of each line is the solubility. CO~2~ (0.067 mL/dL per mm Hg) is far more soluble than O~2~ (0.003), so at a PCO~2~ of 40 about 2.7 mL/dL of CO~2~ is dissolved, while at a PO~2~ of 100 only 0.3 mL/dL of O~2~ is. N~2~ is less soluble than O~2~, and ether is drawn for contrast. The barrier is mostly water, so these solubilities also rank the gases for D. (These rounded values give a ratio of 0.067/0.003 ≈ 22; with unrounded constants it is 22 to 24, and the lecture uses 24.) What the blood does with a gas after it arrives, such as binding it to hemoglobin, is a separate question, in the box below. Course figure.](figures/diffusion/solubility.svg){#fig-diffusion-solubility}

::: {.callout-warning title="A common mistake"}
Two different solubilities matter in this lecture, and they are easy to run together.

- **Solubility in the barrier** is part of D. A gas that dissolves well in the membrane crosses it faster.
- **Solubility or binding in the blood** is not part of D~L~. It sets how fast the partial pressure in the capillary blood rises as the gas arrives. A gas that dissolves well in blood, or binds to something in it, can be taken up in large amounts while its blood partial pressure barely rises. The gradient stays large and the gas keeps moving, but it takes longer to reach equilibrium.

A gas that is soluble in the membrane but poorly soluble in blood equilibrates fastest. CO, which binds hemoglobin, is the extreme case and never equilibrates (later in this chapter).
:::

Helium dissolves very poorly in blood, so almost none of it leaves the lung during a breath-hold or a rebreathing test. That is why it is used to measure lung volumes by helium dilution ([Respiratory Statics](statics.qmd)).

## At least ten layers from alveolus to hemoglobin

Fick's law treats the barrier as one wall. On the way from alveolar gas to hemoglobin, an O~2~ molecule actually crosses at least ten layers (@fig-diffusion-layers): the liquid lining the alveolus; the type I epithelial cell (a membrane, cytoplasm, and another membrane); the interstitium; the capillary endothelial cell (membrane, cytoplasm, membrane); the plasma; and the red cell (membrane and cytoplasm). Not all of them are membranes. Each has its own diffusing capacity, and PO~2~ falls a little across each one.

![The path of O~2~ from alveolar gas to hemoglobin. Layer widths are not to scale. The layers from the surface liquid through the red cell cytoplasm make up the membrane part of the diffusing capacity, D~M~; each is a resistance (1/D), and resistances in series add. Binding to hemoglobin is a final step, θ·V~c~. Course figure, after the lecture's figure redrawn from Boron and Boulpaep [@boron2017].](figures/diffusion/layers.svg){#fig-diffusion-layers}

Each layer is a resistance, one over its diffusing capacity, and resistances in series add. Together the layers from the surface liquid through the red cell make up the *membrane part* of D~L~, written D~M~. Thicken any one of them and D~M~ falls. The interstitium is the layer that thickens in fibrosis and where edema fluid collects first.

Once O~2~ has crossed every membrane it is still only dissolved in the red cell. One more step remains, and it is not a membrane: O~2~ has to combine with hemoglobin. That step acts like one more resistance, the *hemoglobin part*, written θ·V~c~:

- θ is how fast the hemoglobin in 1 mL of blood takes up the gas, per mm Hg. It depends on how fast the gas reacts with hemoglobin and on how much hemoglobin there is.
- V~c~ is the pulmonary capillary blood volume, about 70 mL at rest. Together, θ·V~c~ says how much hemoglobin is exposed to alveolar gas and how fast it binds.

The membrane and hemoglobin parts act in series, so their resistances add:

$$\frac{1}{D_L} = \frac{1}{D_M} + \frac{1}{\theta \cdot V_c}$$

The arithmetic is beyond this course. The idea you need is that the hemoglobin side can limit D~L~ as well as the barrier. Things that lower θ·V~c~ lower D~L~ even when the membrane is normal: anemia (less hemoglobin) and loss of capillary bed, as with a pulmonary embolism (less V~c~). Things that raise θ·V~c~ raise D~L~: exercise recruits and distends pulmonary capillaries and so raises V~c~ (recruitment and distension: [Pulmonary Circulation](../cardiovascular/pulmonary-circulation.qmd)), and polycythemia raises hemoglobin.

### Measuring D~L~ with carbon monoxide

The PFT lab measures the diffusing capacity with carbon monoxide (DLCO), by the single-breath method. The patient takes one breath of a dilute CO mixture, holds it for 10 seconds, and breathes out. The difference between inspired and expired CO gives the rate at which CO disappeared into the blood. CO is used because hemoglobin takes it up so avidly that the capillary PCO stays essentially zero (the next section shows why). The gradient is then simply the alveolar PCO, and the equation collapses to:

$$D_{LCO} = \frac{\dot{V}_{CO}}{P_{ACO}}$$

A normal DLCO is about 25 mL/min/mm Hg. For CO the membrane and hemoglobin resistances are about equal, which is why DLCO falls in anemia and the lab corrects it for the patient's hemoglobin. DLCO rises in exercise because of capillary recruitment and distension. How DLCO helps sort lung diseases is part of [Think Like a Respiratory Consultant](respiratory-consultant.qmd).

## Perfusion limitation and diffusion limitation

Follow a red cell into a pulmonary capillary. It has about 0.75 s to cross at rest. How fast the partial pressure of a gas rises in that blood decides what limits its transfer. @fig-diffusion-perfusion-diffusion shows the two extremes.

![Two ways a gas can behave in the pulmonary capillary, as partial pressure in capillary blood relative to alveolar partial pressure. (A) Nitrous oxide does not bind to hemoglobin, so blood can hold only a little of it and reaches alveolar PN~2~O early; transfer is perfusion limited. (B) Carbon monoxide is taken up by hemoglobin as fast as it arrives, so capillary PCO stays near zero; transfer is diffusion limited. Schematic. Course figure.](figures/diffusion/perfusion-vs-diffusion.svg){#fig-diffusion-perfusion-diffusion}

**Perfusion limited: nitrous oxide (N~2~O).** N~2~O crosses the barrier easily and does not bind to hemoglobin, so blood can hold only a little of it compared with O~2~ or CO. The first N~2~O to cross raises the blood's PN~2~O quickly, and blood and alveolar gas reach equilibrium early in the capillary, well before O~2~ does. After that the gradient is zero and nothing more crosses, however good the barrier is. The only way to take up more N~2~O is to bring more blood, so its uptake is limited by perfusion.

**Diffusion limited: carbon monoxide (CO).** Hemoglobin binds CO so avidly that almost every CO molecule that reaches the red cell is taken up at once, and very little stays free in the plasma. The capillary PCO therefore stays close to zero all the way along, the gradient never closes, and end-capillary PCO is far below alveolar PCO. Uptake is limited by how fast CO can cross the barrier, which is why it is the gas used to measure D~L~.

::: {.callout-warning title="A common mistake"}
It is tempting to think that because CO binds hemoglobin so avidly, the blood must end up with a high PCO. It is the opposite. Partial pressure in blood is set only by the *dissolved* gas. Bound CO does not count, so avid binding keeps PCO near zero, and that is why CO never equilibrates. Its molecular weight (28, lighter than O~2~) has nothing to do with it.
:::

### Where O~2~ and CO~2~ fall

O~2~ lies between the two extremes. It binds hemoglobin, but far less avidly than CO, so capillary PO~2~ does rise. In a normal lung at rest, blood enters at a mixed venous PO~2~ of about 40 and reaches alveolar PO~2~, 100, within about the first third of the capillary, by about 0.25 s (@fig-diffusion-o2-co2). For the remaining two thirds no more O~2~ moves. At rest, O~2~ transfer is perfusion limited, and the unused length of the capillary is a large *diffusion reserve*.

CO~2~ moves the other way: blood enters at a mixed venous PCO~2~ of about 46 mm Hg (slide 15 rounds it to 45) and falls to the alveolar 40 in about the same time. CO~2~ is perfusion limited too. Its gradient is only about 6 mm Hg, roughly a tenth of the starting gradient for O~2~, so its 20-fold higher diffusivity is what lets it equilibrate just as quickly. "40 to 100 for O~2~, 46 to 40 for CO~2~" are good anchor numbers.

![Capillary PO~2~ and PCO~2~ in a normal lung at rest. (A) O~2~: blood enters at 40 mm Hg and reaches alveolar PO~2~ (100) well within the first third of the 0.75 s transit; the shaded part is the diffusion reserve. (B) CO~2~: blood enters at about 46 mm Hg and falls to the alveolar 40 in about the same time. The O~2~ curve comes from a simple model of O~2~ loading that uses the course's dissociation curve; the CO~2~ curve is schematic. Course figure.](figures/diffusion/o2-co2-equilibration.svg){#fig-diffusion-o2-co2}

Look at the shape of the O~2~ curve. It starts slowly, then rises steeply, then flattens. The flattening is the gradient closing as capillary PO~2~ approaches alveolar PO~2~. The slow start comes from hemoglobin. Between 40 and 60 mm Hg the blood is on the steep part of the O~2~ dissociation curve, where hemoglobin takes up a large amount of O~2~ for each mm Hg rise in PO~2~. Most of the O~2~ that crosses the barrier binds to hemoglobin instead of raising plasma PO~2~, so PO~2~ climbs slowly at first. Above about 60 mm Hg the dissociation curve is flat, hemoglobin is nearly full, and each bit of O~2~ that crosses raises PO~2~ quickly. This is the same reason CO equilibrates slowly, in a milder form. Hemoglobin's affinity for O~2~ is not lower on the steep part of the curve.

## When O~2~ becomes diffusion limited

The reserve can be used up in three ways: a thicker barrier (low D~L~), less time in the capillary, or a smaller gradient. @fig-diffusion-reserve shows all three.

![Capillary PO~2~ along the capillary for a normal diffusing capacity and for a D~L~ of one quarter and one eighth of normal. (A) At sea level, the normal lung equilibrates early, and even with the 0.25 s transit of heavy exercise it still reaches alveolar PO~2~. A lung with a low D~L~ reaches equilibrium only late or not at all, and with a short transit it leaves the capillary well below alveolar PO~2~. (B) At altitude (13,500 ft, alveolar PO~2~ about 50, mixed venous about 25) the gradient is smaller and the blood loads on the steep part of the dissociation curve, so even the normal lung needs most of the transit time and falls short with exercise. Curves from the same model as @fig-diffusion-o2-co2, after the figures from West's *Respiratory Physiology* [@west2016] used in the 2026 lecture. The model holds D~L~ constant. Real blood binds O~2~ faster when hemoglobin is less saturated, so at altitude the normal lung equilibrates somewhat sooner than drawn: slide 22 shows it equilibrating by about 0.45 s. Both show the normal lung falling short when transit is cut to 0.25 s.](figures/diffusion/diffusion-reserve.svg){#fig-diffusion-reserve}

**A thickened barrier.** In pulmonary fibrosis, scar thickens the alveolar walls and interstitium, the diffusion path lengthens, and D~L~ falls. Capillary PO~2~ rises more slowly. If the gradient has not closed by the time the blood leaves, transfer is diffusion limited: blood that entered at 40 might leave at 80 while alveolar PO~2~ is 100. End-capillary PO~2~ ends below alveolar PO~2~, which raises the A–a gradient. A very abnormal lung is diffusion limited even at rest.

**Exercise: less time.** During exercise cardiac output rises, and because all the blood must pass through the lungs, the transit time through the pulmonary capillaries can fall to about 0.25 s. A normal lung at sea level still equilibrates, so in most healthy people the lung at sea level stays perfusion limited even with hard exercise. A lung with a low D~L~ no longer has time, and blood leaves well below alveolar PO~2~. This is why a patient with interstitial lung disease can look fine sitting in a chair and desaturate walking down the hall, and why clinicians check O~2~ saturation during exercise, often with a six-minute walk test.

**Altitude: a smaller gradient.** Fick's law says transfer is proportional to the partial pressure difference. At altitude FiO~2~ is still 0.21, but P~B~ is lower, so inspired and alveolar PO~2~ are lower. At 13,500 feet PAO~2~ is about 50 and mixed venous PO~2~ is roughly 20 to 25, so the starting gradient is about 25 to 30 mm Hg instead of 60. The blood is also loading on the steep part of the dissociation curve the whole way, which slows the rise in PO~2~ further. At rest the normal lung still just equilibrates. With exertion, transit time falls and end-capillary PO~2~ stays below alveolar PO~2~. Strenuous exercise at altitude is one of the few situations that makes a healthy person diffusion limited.

**Combinations.** In patients it is usually a combination: a thickened barrier plus exertion, or lung disease plus altitude, including the cabin of an airliner pressurized to 7,000 ft.

::: {.callout-note title="If you are comparing with the slides"}
The 2025 Diffusion notes (section IX) have a column "Response to 100% O~2~" in the perfusion versus diffusion limitation table. Ignore that column. Perfusion and diffusion limitation describe whether a gas reaches equilibrium before the blood leaves the capillary, a property that applies to every gas, and a response to O~2~ means nothing for N~2~O, CO~2~ or CO. Hypoxemia from diffusion limitation does improve with supplemental O~2~, because a higher PAO~2~ widens the gradient across the barrier. The [Ventilation and Perfusion](ventilation-perfusion.qmd) chapter sorts the causes of hypoxemia by their response to O~2~.
:::

### A question from Everest

In 2009, Grocott and colleagues drew arterial blood from healthy climbers at 8,400 m on Everest, breathing ambient air [@w10-grocott2009]. Barometric pressure was 272 mm Hg. Inspired PO~2~ was 0.21 × (272 − 47) ≈ 47 mm Hg, and hyperventilation had driven PaCO~2~ down to about 13, so by the alveolar gas equation PAO~2~ was about 47 − 13/0.8 ≈ 30 mm Hg. The measured arterial PO~2~ averaged 24.6 mm Hg, below the alveolar value. At sea level capillary PO~2~ reaches alveolar PO~2~. Why didn't it up there?

The gradient that drives O~2~ across the barrier starts out tiny, smaller even than in @fig-diffusion-reserve B, and the blood is loading on the steepest part of the dissociation curve. Capillary PO~2~ rises slowly and runs out of transit time before it reaches alveolar PO~2~, worse with any exertion. Most likely, at this altitude O~2~ transfer becomes diffusion limited even in a healthy lung.

This does not change how altitude is classified. At rest, altitude is a cause of hypoxemia from a low PAO~2~ with a normal A–a gradient, which is how the [Alveolar Ventilation](ventilation.qmd) chapter and Small Group 2 count it. Diffusion limitation appears on top of that when transit time shortens, as in exercise at altitude, or at the most extreme altitudes. Small Group 2 uses one climber from the same camp as a teaching case with round numbers: PaCO~2~ 12, PAO~2~ 32 and PaO~2~ 30 mm Hg, an A–a gradient of 2. The [transport chapter](o2-co2-transport.qmd) uses him.

## Check your understanding

1. A disease halves the alveolar surface area and also doubles the thickness of the barrier. By how much does O~2~ transfer change if the gradient is unchanged? Which term of the diffusing capacity changed?

    <details><summary>Answer</summary>

    V̇~gas~ ∝ A·D/T × (P~1~ − P~2~). Halving A halves transfer, and doubling T halves it again, so transfer falls to a quarter. Both changes are in the membrane part of D~L~ (D~M~). In reality the gradient would not stay fixed: as transfer fell, end-capillary PO~2~ would fall below alveolar PO~2~ if the reserve ran out.

    </details>

2. The starting gradient for CO~2~ in the pulmonary capillary is only about 6 mm Hg, against about 60 for O~2~. Why does CO~2~ still equilibrate as fast as O~2~?

    <details><summary>Answer</summary>

    CO~2~ is about 24 times as soluble as O~2~ in the barrier and only slightly heavier, so its diffusion constant is about 20 times higher. Per mm Hg of gradient it crosses about 20 times faster, which more than makes up for a gradient about a tenth as large. That is why CO~2~ is almost never diffusion limited.

    </details>

3. A healthy runner's D~L~ is higher during a race than at rest. Which part of the diffusing capacity changed, and why?

    <details><summary>Answer</summary>

    The hemoglobin part, θ·V~c~. Exercise raises cardiac output and pulmonary pressures, which recruit closed capillaries and distend open ones, so capillary blood volume (V~c~) rises and more hemoglobin is exposed to alveolar gas. The membrane is unchanged. (The larger exposed surface from recruitment also helps D~M~ a little.)

    </details>

4. In a resting subject, N~2~O uptake doubles when cardiac output doubles. Why? Would a moderately thickened alveolar barrier change N~2~O uptake?

    <details><summary>Answer</summary>

    N~2~O does not bind hemoglobin, so blood can hold only a little of it, and capillary PN~2~O reaches alveolar PN~2~O early in the capillary. After that the gradient is zero and nothing more crosses. Each milliliter of blood leaves carrying the same small amount, so uptake is set by how much blood passes: twice the flow carries away twice as much. A higher cardiac output shortens the transit time somewhat, but N~2~O equilibrates so early that the shorter time is still enough. A moderately thickened barrier slows equilibration, but as long as the blood still reaches alveolar PN~2~O before it leaves the capillary, uptake does not change. Only a barrier so thick that equilibrium is never reached would make N~2~O uptake depend on the barrier.

    </details>

5. If alveolar PO~2~ and arterial PO~2~ are both about 100 mm Hg, where is the gradient that moves O~2~ into the blood?

    <details><summary>Answer</summary>

    Along the capillary. Blood enters at a mixed venous PO~2~ of about 40, so the gradient is about 60 mm Hg at the start, and it shrinks to almost zero about a third of the way along as hemoglobin fills. P~2~ in Fick's law is capillary PO~2~ averaged along the capillary, not the arterial value.

    </details>

6. Why does capillary PO~2~ rise slowly over the first part of the capillary, then quickly, then level off?

    <details><summary>Answer</summary>

    Only dissolved O~2~ sets PO~2~. At first the blood is on the steep part of the dissociation curve, so most of the O~2~ that crosses binds to hemoglobin and PO~2~ rises slowly. Once PO~2~ passes about 60 mm Hg, hemoglobin is nearly full, little O~2~ is bound per mm Hg, and PO~2~ rises fast. It levels off as it nears alveolar PO~2~ and the gradient closes.

    </details>

## Key equations

| Equation | Use |
|---|---|
| V̇~gas~ = (A·D/T)(P~1~ − P~2~) | Fick's law of diffusion |
| D ∝ solubility/√MW | Diffusion constant; CO~2~ ≈ 20 × O~2~ |
| V̇~gas~ = D~L~ (P~1~ − P~2~) | Fick's law for the lung |
| 1/D~L~ = 1/D~M~ + 1/(θ·V~c~) | Membrane and hemoglobin parts (concept only) |
| D~LCO~ = V̇~CO~/P~ACO~ | DLCO, because capillary PCO stays near zero; normal about 25 mL/min/mm Hg |
